Human & machine perception

What makes two shapes look alike?

A model can recognize every small shape in an image and still disagree with people about which ones look similar. Explore what changed across six vision checkpoints.

Human visual search

Which differences do people see?

Eight people searched for a target among distractors. Faster searches indicate easier distinctions. For each model, we compared the ranking of its embedding distances with the human ranking across pairs of the 49 images above.

Agreement with human search speed

Base is the original checkpoint. UnAligNet learns from a teacher’s image similarities. AligNet learns from teacher similarities adjusted using human judgments. Comparing the last two addresses the proposal’s alignment question.

Where the numbers come from. The frozen checkpoints are the official weights released by the AligNet authors. The Navon scores are from this project. For example, 0.258 and 0.526 are the scores of the released SigLIP-B UnAligNet and AligNet checkpoints on the same 147 pairs where only the small elements changed. Those scores use pre_logits before any reweighting.

Inside the representations

Recognition and similarity can move independently.

SigLIP knows the elements

All three checkpoints identified the small element in 49 of 49 images with a linear classifier tested on unfamiliar outlines. Yet for pairs changing only the small element, agreement rose from 0.258 in UnAligNet to 0.526 in AligNet.

Among 21 element substitutions, people ranked square versus N 12th in dissimilarity. UnAligNet ranked it 20th. AligNet ranked it 12th.

DINOv2’s outline drop starts with UnAligNet

The outline probe got 43 of 49 images right with Base, 21 of 49 with UnAligNet, and 23 of 49 with AligNet. In human visual search, agreement on outline-only changes also fell sharply from Base to UnAligNet, then partly recovered with AligNet.

This is why the project compares AligNet with UnAligNet. The teacher-trained checkpoint already showed the largest drop, before accounting for the human-aligned teacher targets.

Which image looks closer to the reference?

A model turns each image into a vector of numbers. If changing the outline moves that vector only a little, an outline change contributes little to the distance between images. A probe trained to read the outline can still pick up that small, consistent signal.

What the DINOv2 probes found

We tested 49 controlled images, holding out one type of small shape at a time. When the probe kept track of patch locations, it identified the outline in 49 of 49 images for Base and 47 of 49 for UnAligNet. Reading the final image vector, it got 44 and 29 right. These fixed layouts show how much outline information a probe can recover at each stage.

On the human visual-search task, agreement for outline-only changes fell from 0.747 in Base to 0.435 in UnAligNet and recovered to 0.592 in AligNet. One possible explanation is that training on photographs rewards cues that usually occur together. Navon images pull those cues apart. The probes locate a difference in how accessible the outline is. Establishing which training choices caused it requires a controlled training comparison.

Transfer and feature weighting

The SigLIP gain carries over to a second human task.

In a separate experiment, 16 participants judged whether two images shared the same small element or overall outline. We ran all six checkpoints on the original stimuli and compared frozen distances with inverse mean response time. Each Navon row uses 147 pairs where only the named cue changed.

The project proposal

Does learning human concepts help a model see shapes better?

On these stimuli, the human-aligned SigLIP checkpoint better predicts which element changes people distinguish easily. DINOv2 shows little overall change from UnAligNet. The 1,176 pairs share just 49 images, and these differences are descriptive.

The proposal tests transfer through four additional questions: conceptual agreement on Levels, matching unfamiliar outlines after rotation or translation, clean object recognition, and choices when object shape and texture disagree. The shape study adds a human perceptual measure alongside those planned tests.
